memory_candidates.content: Bash pitfall: capturing a command's own exit code via `$?` immediately after `X=$(cmd | grep ... | sort -u)` captures the LAST pipeline command's exit status (e.g. sort -u's, almost always 0), not `cmd`'s -- because the pipeline runs inside the command substitution's own subshell, and that subshell's PIPESTATUS array does not propagate back to the parent shell. This silently defeats any downstream branching on `cmd`'s real exit code (e.g. distinguishing exit 0/1/2 for a baseline-comparison mechanism). Fix: capture the target command's exit code FIRST, as the sole command in its own substitution (`RAW=$(cmd); EXIT=$?`), then filter/transform the already-captured text as a separate subsequent step (`FILTERED=$(printf '%s\n' "$RAW" | grep ... | sort -u)`). Caught empirically during verification by running the documented one-liner and observing EXIT=0 despite the wrapped command actually failing.

When a caller needs to extend fail()/error-recording helper to also feed a machine-diffable findings accumulator, giving the helper an optional Nth argument that OVERRIDES (or, if passed empty string, SUPPRESSES) the default recorded text is more robust than assuming the human-facing message is always fit for machine comparison. Two recurring needs surfaced: (1) a message embedding a numeric count must be normalized count-free before use as a diff key, since magnitude drift inside an already-failing check must not manufacture a spurious 'new' finding; (2) an aggregate 'N things failed, see detail' message should be suppressed in favor of N separately-extracted per-underlying-finding lines, to avoid one redundant generic finding riding alongside the real ones. Distinguish 'argument omitted' from 'argument passed empty' via $# inside the function, not just truthiness of the value, so both behaviors (override vs. suppress) are reachable through one optional parameter.
